name: Critical Raw Materials Act
evidence_rating: thin: early stock-takes of the strategic-project pipeline (Bruegel: targets met for only five materials; delays in Global South projects) and a critical ECA audit; no causal studies
summary: The Act set 2030 goals for the EU to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the strategic raw materials it uses, and to rely on no single country for more than 65%. The Commission has designated 47 EU Strategic Projects with EUR 22.5 billion of planned investment, but the European Court of Auditors concluded in 2026 that the goals are unlikely to be met. No study has yet measured the Act's effect on supply security or prices.

indicators.objective: Strengthen the strategic raw materials value chain
indicators.indicator: EU capacity as share of annual EU consumption of strategic raw materials by 2030
indicators.target_or_baseline: Extraction 10%, processing 40%, recycling 25%; no more than 65% from a single third country
indicators.evidence: European Court of Auditors (Feb 2026) judges the EU unlikely to meet the 2030 benchmarks: targets are non-binding, unclear in basis, mining projects take up to two decades, and 10 of 26 energy-transition materials are not recycled at all.

indicators.indicator: Number of Strategic Projects financed in the EU and abroad; investment volume
indicators.evidence: 47 EU Strategic Projects selected in March 2025 (expected capital investment EUR 22.5bn; 25 extraction, 24 processing, 10 recycling, 2 substitution), further third-country projects in June 2025 and a second call in Sept 2025. Investment actually made not reported.

indicators.indicator: Monitoring data on trade flows in CRMs
indicators.evidence: ECA found imports from the 14 strategic-partner countries fell between 2020 and 2024 for around half of materials examined.

indicators.indicator: Amount and share of recycled CRMs
indicators.evidence: ECA: recycling still in its infancy; no Commission measurement yet.

indicators.indicator: Data and maps of EU mineral resources; strategic stocks at national level

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Impact Assessment accompanying the Critical Raw Materials Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2023) 162), SWD(2023) 161
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Critical Raw Materials Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2023) 162)
literature.headline: Preferred option (Strategic Projects with streamlined permitting and finance) expected to help meet EU capacity targets and benefit downstream competitiveness; benefits and costs described qualitatively, IA notes the more ambitious option would have been more effective
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected Strategic Projects and faster permits to raise EU capacity in critical raw materials, but gave no headline economic figures.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Commission selects 47 Strategic Projects to secure and diversify access to raw materials in the EU, Press release, 25 March 2025 (as reported by Global Mining Review)
literature.title: Commission selects 47 Strategic Projects to secure and diversify access to raw materials in the EU
literature.venue: Press release, 25 March 2025 (as reported by Global Mining Review)
literature.headline: 47 projects in 13 Member States, expected capital investment EUR 22.5bn, covering 14 of 17 strategic raw materials (22 lithium projects)
literature.summary_plain: In March 2025 the Commission designated 47 EU mining, processing and recycling projects with EUR 22.5 billion of planned investment.
literature.quality: activity data; planned not realised investment

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2026), Special report 04/2026: Critical raw materials for the energy transition - Not a rock-solid policy, European Court of Auditors
literature.title: Special report 04/2026: Critical raw materials for the energy transition - Not a rock-solid policy
literature.method: performance audit (document review, trade data, project analysis)
literature.headline: EU unlikely to secure sufficient strategic raw materials by 2030; CRMA targets non-binding with unclear methodology; imports from strategic partners fell for about half of materials 2020-2024; permitting delays and energy costs hold back domestic projects
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors concluded the EU is unlikely to hit its 2030 raw-materials goals: diversification has produced little and recycling is in its infancy.

literature.authors: Madalena Barata da Rocha, Antoine Mathieu Collin, Camille Reverdy
literature.title: Competing for inputs: how the European Union can improve critical raw materials supply security
literature.method: descriptive analysis of the 60 CRMA strategic projects (allocation vs projected demand and China import dependency; promoter-reported output as share of forecast 2030 EU demand) plus trade-data analysis (CEPII BACI) of strategic partnerships and FTA CRM provisions
literature.outcomes: alignment of strategic projects with demand and dependencies; projected contribution to CRMA 2030 benchmarks; trade effects of partnerships
literature.headline: Strategic projects could cover the CRMA extraction and processing targets for only five CRMs in a low-demand scenario and probably not the recycling target; project allocation shows no systematic link to import dependency on China, and strategic partnerships show no measurable trade effects yet.
literature.summary_plain: Bruegel looked at the 60 projects the EU has labelled 'strategic' under the Act and found they are unlikely to make the EU self-sufficient by 2030 and do not target the materials where dependence on China is greatest. Trade agreements have so far done more to raise supplies to the EU.
literature.quality: Descriptive and early; relies on unverified promoter output projections (authors warn of overstatement incentives); no counterfactual for CRMA itself.
literature.citation: Madalena Barata da Rocha, Antoine Mathieu Collin, Camille Reverdy (2026), Competing for inputs: how the European Union can improve critical raw materials supply security, Bruegel Policy Brief 15/2026 (9 July 2026)

literature.title: Batteries Not Included: The EU's Strategic Raw Material Projects in the Global South
literature.venue: Munich Security Analysis 2/2026, Munich Security Conference (August 2026); doi:10.47342/vzmd6856
literature.method: structured qualitative assessment of the six CRMA strategic projects in the Global South against partner-country conditions (processing investment, technology transfer, risk absorption), with project status table
literature.outcomes: progress and value-addition features of non-EU strategic projects
literature.headline: Of the six CRMA strategic projects in the Global South, three are listed as delayed, and the EU is judged to be struggling to deliver processing investment, technology transfer and risk-absorption finance that partners demand.
literature.summary_plain: The paper checks the EU's 'strategic' raw-material projects in Africa, Asia and Latin America and finds several are behind schedule and the EU is not delivering the local processing and financing support partner countries want.
literature.period_geography: 2025-2026; Brazil, Zambia, Kazakhstan, Madagascar, Malawi, South Africa
literature.quality: Small set of cases; qualitative assessment drawing on secondary sources and MSC meetings; no quantitative outcome measure.
literature.citation: Nora Kürzdörfer (2026), Batteries Not Included: The EU's Strategic Raw Material Projects in the Global South, Munich Security Analysis 2/2026, Munich Security Conference (August 2026); doi:10.47342/vzmd6856

literature.title: The EU's Raw Materials Strategic Projects: First Results
literature.venue: World Economy and International Relations (Mirovaya ekonomika i mezhdunarodnye otnosheniya), vol. 70, no. 9, pp. 36-44
literature.method: descriptive analysis of the first-round CRMA strategic projects (type, materials, location, brownfield vs greenfield) and their links to EU trade and partnership instruments
literature.outcomes: composition of first strategic projects; diversification of suppliers
literature.headline: The first CRMA strategic projects favour existing or restarted operations over greenfield investment and are concentrated in countries already tied to the EU through Global Gateway, CRM partnerships and trade agreements.
literature.summary_plain: A review of the first projects chosen under the Act finds the EU mostly picked mines and plants that already exist or are being reopened, rather than new ones, and mainly in countries it already works with.
literature.quality: Descriptive only; no numbers in abstract; published by IMEMO (Russian Academy of Sciences institute); abstract obtained via Crossref because publisher page blocked access.
literature.citation: A. Chetverikova (2026), The EU's Raw Materials Strategic Projects: First Results, World Economy and International Relations (Mirovaya ekonomika i mezhdunarodnye otnosheniya), vol. 70, no. 9, pp. 36-44

literature.title: Strategic projects for whom? Challenges and local realities of the European Union's strategic mineral projects
literature.method: survey of the 13 promoters of non-EU strategic projects (4 responded) plus web research and the BHRC Transition Minerals Tracker allegations database
literature.outcomes: human-rights policies, impact assessments and abuse allegations linked to strategic project promoters
literature.headline: None of the 13 promoters of non-EU strategic projects has both a public human rights policy and a project impact assessment; only 4 of 13 answered BHRC, and at least 4 of 13 are linked to past allegations of abuse.
literature.summary_plain: A human-rights group asked the companies behind the EU's overseas 'strategic' mining projects about their safeguards; most did not reply and none had both a human rights policy and a published impact assessment for the project.
literature.quality: Simple descriptive audit with low response rate; campaigning perspective; does not measure on-the-ground outcomes.
literature.interested_party: campaigning NGO on business and human rights
literature.citation: Business & Human Rights Resource Centre (2025), Strategic projects for whom? Challenges and local realities of the European Union's strategic mineral projects, BHRC Briefing

evidence_rating_previous: ex-ante plus early audit: Commission activity data and a critical ECA audit; no causal study
